script.opening: (The doctor rings you and starts by saying there has been a mistake with your medication.) "A mistake? What do you mean? Is it serious? I've been taking my tablets like it said on the box…"

facts.text: Maureen Selby, 67. You have rheumatoid arthritis and have taken methotrexate "once a week, on a Monday" for three years, with folic acid on another day.
Your new box from the chemist last week said "take ONE tablet DAILY". You thought the dose had been changed, so you have taken one every day for six days. You are holding the box while you talk.
A couple of mouth ulcers since yesterday, a bit queasy, more tired than usual. No fever, no sore throat, no bruising or bleeding, no breathlessness or cough, no diarrhoea.
Folic acid once a week, paracetamol when needed. No allergies.
Lives with your husband Bill, who can drive. Retired dinner lady.

facts.topic: Feelings — reveal as the call goes on
facts.text: First shock and fear: "Am I going to be alright?" Then self-blame: "I should have known — it's always been weekly." Then some anger: "How did nobody notice?" If the doctor is defensive or vague, the anger grows: "I want to make a complaint."

Listen. If the doctor explains clearly what happened, says sorry plainly, tells you it was not your fault and tells you exactly what to do now (stop the tablets, blood test today, what symptoms to watch for), you calm down and cooperate. Ask: "Will this have damaged anything?" and "How do I know it won't happen again?" If they minimise ("it's probably fine") or blame the pharmacy without taking responsibility, become angry.

ice.ideas: "I've been taking them exactly as the box said."
ice.concerns: "Is it serious? Have I poisoned myself?" Also: "Was this my fault?" and anger that it happened at all.
ice.expectations: To know exactly what happened, whether you are in danger and what to do now. You also want to know it will not happen again to you or anyone else.

cues: "I took them like it said on the box." — say early.
"I've got a couple of mouth ulcers, actually." — say when asked how you feel.
"How do I know it won't happen again?" — ask near the end.

checkpoints.text: Acts URGENTLY on the clinical risk: recognises daily methotrexate for ~6 days as potentially serious toxicity — advises STOPPING the drug immediately, arranges urgent bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs), assesses for toxicity (mucositis, GI, infection/bleeding, breathlessness), and seeks urgent specialist/toxicology advice (folinic acid rescue, possible admission) even though she feels well so far

Fulfils the DUTY OF CANDOUR (CQC Regulation 20; GMC/NMC professional duty of candour 2015): discloses the error promptly, honestly and FULLY — what happened, that it was a mistake, and the potential consequences — without minimising, hiding or being defensive
APOLOGISES sincerely and clearly (recognising an apology is not an admission of legal liability), and explains what will be done now and to prevent recurrence
LIFTS the patient’s self-blame: makes explicit that this was the system/prescriber’s error, NOT her fault — she took it exactly as labelled — countering the "I took it like it said" self-blame

Commits to the SYSTEM response: reporting/significant event analysis, understanding how it happened and fixing it (prescribing/dispensing safeguards), and checking no other patients are affected — and tells her this
Delivers the disclosure with compassion and calm, takes responsibility on behalf of the practice without defensiveness, and manages her fear/anger empathically
Keeps her informed and supported throughout, checks her understanding and feelings, and gives her a clear point of contact — treating her as a partner in putting it right, not a problem to be managed

Safety-nets robustly: urgent bloods/assessment and the toxicity red flags to act on (mouth ulcers, fever/infection, bruising/bleeding, breathlessness → urgent/999), the plan and follow-up, written information, named contact, documentation of the candour conversation, an offer to meet in person, and the written notification with the apology and an update on enquiries (CQC Regulation 20)

worked.txt: "I’m really sorry, Mrs Selby — I need to be completely straight with you. Your methotrexate should be taken just ONCE A WEEK, but because of a mistake on our side it was issued as a DAILY dose, and you’ve been taking it every day for about six days. That’s our error, not yours, and I’m telling you straight away so we can put it right immediately."

"I want to apologise properly — this should not have happened, and I’m sorry for the worry it’s going to cause you. This is something we got wrong, and it’s our job to fix it and to make sure it can’t happen to anyone else."

"And please hear this clearly: you did absolutely nothing wrong. You took the tablets exactly as they were labelled — anyone would have. This is not your fault in any way. So don’t carry an ounce of blame for this."

"Now, the important bit — what we do about it. Please STOP the methotrexate now, don’t take any more. Taken daily it can affect your blood counts and your mouth and tummy, so I need you to have some urgent blood tests today, and I’m going to get specialist advice straight away — there’s a treatment that can protect you if needed, and occasionally we admit people to be safe. You feel well now, which is good, but we act anyway because it’s the safe thing."

"Watch for these and tell us urgently, or go to A&E: mouth ulcers, a sore mouth or throat, a fever or any sign of infection, easy bruising or bleeding, or getting breathless. Any of those, don’t wait. I’ll give you a number to reach us directly."

"Beyond you, I’m reporting this so we understand exactly how it happened and change our system so it can’t happen again, and we’re checking no one else has been affected. I’d also like to meet you in person once you’re safe, and I’ll send you a written account of what happened with our apology. I’ll personally keep you updated, I’ll chase your blood results today, and you can ring me directly. I’m sorry again — you trusted us, and we’ll work hard to put this right and keep you safe."

f.learning: A methotrexate dose issued DAILY instead of WEEKLY — taken for ~6 days — is a classic, potentially fatal prescribing error, and the consultation has two inseparable strands. Clinically: act URGENTLY despite the patient feeling well — stop the drug, urgent bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs), assess for toxicity (mucositis, GI upset, marrow suppression/infection/bleeding, pneumonitis), and seek specialist/toxicology advice (folinic acid rescue, possible admission), with clear toxicity red-flag safety-netting. Ethically: fulfil the DUTY OF CANDOUR (CQC Regulation 20; GMC/NMC 2015) — disclose promptly, honestly and fully, APOLOGISE sincerely (an apology is not an admission of legal liability), explain what happened and what will be done, follow the call with an offer to meet in person and a written account including the apology, keep a record, and commit to a system response (significant event analysis, fixing the prescribing/dispensing safeguard, checking other patients). The examinable skills are doing this WITHOUT defensiveness or minimising, and managing the patient’s fear and self-blame — explicitly lifting the "I took it like it said" self-blame (it was the system’s error, not hers) — while keeping her informed, supported and treated as a partner in putting it right.

knowledge.guideline: MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020) — methotrexate once-weekly · CQC Regulation 20 duty of candour · GMC and NMC professional duty of candour (2015) · NICE NG253 (sepsis)
knowledge.summary: Daily instead of weekly methotrexate is a recognised, potentially fatal error. Stop it, get same-day bloods and specialist advice, and disclose it openly with an apology in the same call.

points.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020): methotrexate for autoimmune disease is taken once a week, and fatal overdoses continue to be reported from daily dosing. Toxicity includes mucositis, diarrhoea and vomiting, bone-marrow suppression (neutropenic sepsis, bleeding), liver injury, renal impairment and pneumonitis. Symptoms may lag behind blood changes, so feeling well is not reassurance.

Stop methotrexate now and remove the remaining supply. Arrange same-day FBC, U&E and LFTs with clinical assessment, and seek urgent specialist advice (acute medical or rheumatology team, using TOXBASE/National Poisons Information Service guidance). Calcium folinate rescue and admission are specialist decisions — doses per BNF and specialist advice.

Neutropenia after methotrexate overdose can present as fever or simply feeling unwell. Any fever, rigors, sore throat or feeling acutely unwell needs emergency assessment as possible neutropenic sepsis (NICE NG253 for people aged 16 and over).

CQC Regulation 20 applies to registered providers, including GP practices. For a notifiable safety incident (one that has caused, or might cause, moderate or severe harm or death) the practice must tell the person, give a true account, apologise, explain what enquiries will follow, confirm it in writing and keep a record. CQC expects the notification in person; an urgent phone call is right here, followed by an offer to meet and a written account.

GMC and NMC guidance on the professional duty of candour (2015) and GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): be open and honest, apologise, explain the short- and long-term effects, and put matters right. An apology is not an admission of legal liability (Compensation Act 2006, section 2; NHS Resolution “Saying sorry”, 2017).

Record and report the incident (local reporting and the national Learn from Patient Safety Events service), hold a significant event analysis, check that no other patient has received the same directions, and fix the safeguard. MHRA advice: agree the day of the week with the patient and write it in full on the prescription.

dg.d: Confirmed identity, checked it was a good time to talk, and stated the purpose of the call plainly at the outset.
Ability to attend today, practical support, and how she is coping with the shock.
Same-day FBC, U&E and LFTs with clinical assessment; tablets retained for checking.
Screens for mucositis, GI toxicity, marrow suppression, liver or renal injury and pneumonitis; asks about interacting medicines.
Recognises possible neutropenic sepsis and bleeding risk; does not accept “I feel fine” as reassurance.
States clearly: a prescribing error with around six days of daily methotrexate, potentially serious, currently without symptoms.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop the drug now, same-day bloods, urgent specialist advice (folinic acid rescue, possible admission), with her agreement.
Fulfils the duty of candour: apology, true account, incident report, significant event analysis, checks other patients, written follow-up.
Named red flags with 999/A&E route, direct contact number, timed call-back, and results chased the same day.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I took it like it said” (self-blame) and “I’m a bit cross” (anger), and responded to each.
Her understanding of the error, her fear of harm, her anger at being let down, and what she wants to happen.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "Is it serious? Have I poisoned myself?" Also: "Was this my fault?" and anger that it happened at all — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Maureen Selby? It’s Dr Patel from the surgery. Before I go on, could you confirm your date of birth for me, please?
model.why: Confirms identity before disclosing clinical information by phone

model.text: Yes, that’s me. Is something wrong?

Thank you. I’m ringing because I need to be honest with you about a mistake we’ve made with your medication, and to sort it out with you straight away. Is now an okay time, and are you somewhere you can talk?
model.why: Signals the purpose clearly and checks it is a safe moment to talk

model.text: A mistake? What do you mean? Is it serious? I’ve been taking my tablets like it said…

I’m going to be completely straight with you. Your methotrexate should only ever be taken once a week. On your last prescription the instructions were wrong — they said every day — and I understand you’ve been taking it daily for about six days. That was our error, and I’m very sorry.
model.why: Full, prompt, factual disclosure with a clear apology — the core of the duty of candour

model.text: Oh my goodness. I did exactly what the label said. Have I done something stupid?
No — please hear this clearly. You did nothing wrong at all. You followed the label exactly, as anyone would. The mistake was ours, not yours.
model.why: Responds to the self-blame cue immediately and lifts it

model.text: But is it dangerous? Am I going to be alright?

It can be serious, which is why I’m ringing today rather than writing. Taken daily, methotrexate can lower your blood counts and affect your mouth, stomach, liver and kidneys. The good news is that we’ve caught it, and there are checks and a treatment that can protect you. First, though, can I ask how you are feeling?
model.why: Honest about risk without catastrophising, then moves to assess toxicity

model.text: Have you had any mouth ulcers or a sore mouth or throat, any sickness or diarrhoea, a temperature or shivers, any unusual bruising or bleeding, or a cough or breathlessness?
model.why: Screens systematically for mucositis, GI toxicity, marrow suppression and pneumonitis

model.text: No, nothing like that. I feel quite well, really. That’s why I didn’t think anything was wrong.
That’s good to hear. The blood effects can show up before you feel anything, though, so we still need to act today. Do you still have the tablets with you?
model.why: Explains why feeling well does not remove the need to act

model.text: Yes, the box is here in the kitchen.
Please don’t take any more — stop them from now. Put the box to one side so it can be checked. Are you taking any other medicines at the moment that I should know about?
model.why: Stops the drug, secures the supply and checks for interacting medicines

model.text: Just what’s on my list at the surgery.

Here’s what I’d like to happen today. You need blood tests this afternoon to check your blood count, kidneys and liver. I’m also going to speak to the hospital specialist team straight after this call. There’s an antidote-type treatment called folinic acid that they may want to give, and they may prefer to see you at the hospital today to be safe. Can you get there if needed?
model.why: Same-day bloods and specialist advice; names folinic acid rescue and possible admission

model.text: I can get there, yes. Hospital, though? That frightens me.

I understand — it sounds alarming. Going in doesn’t mean something bad has happened; it means we’re being careful because the mistake was ours and we want to catch any effect early. What’s going through your mind right now?
model.why: Acknowledges fear and invites her feelings rather than rushing on

model.text: I just trusted you. I’m shaken, and a bit cross, honestly.
You have every right to feel cross. You trusted us and we let you down. I’m not going to make excuses — I’m going to make sure you’re safe and keep you informed at every step.
model.why: Accepts her anger without defensiveness and takes responsibility for the practice

model.text: I also want you to know what happens next on our side. We’re reporting this as a patient-safety incident, we’ll look at exactly how the wrong instructions got through, and we’re checking no one else has been affected. I’ll write to you with what we find and what we change, and I’d like to offer you a meeting in person once you’re safe.
model.why: Commits to reporting, significant event analysis, checking other patients and written follow-up

model.text: I’d want to know it can’t happen to anyone else.
That’s exactly what we want too, and I’ll tell you what we’ve changed. In future your prescription will state the day of the week you take it, written in full.
model.why: Links her request to a concrete safeguard

model.text: Until you’re seen, if you get a temperature, shivers or feel suddenly unwell, a sore mouth or throat, bleeding or bruising, or breathlessness — ring 999 or go straight to A&E and tell them you’ve had extra methotrexate. I’ll give you my direct line for anything else.
model.why: Specific toxicity and sepsis red flags with a clear route

model.text: All right. I’ll write that down.
Could you tell me back what you’re going to do this afternoon, just so I know I’ve explained it well?
No more tablets, blood test today, wait for your call about the hospital, and 999 if I get a temperature or bleeding.

That’s exactly right. I’ll ring you back within the hour once I’ve spoken to the specialists, and I’ll chase your results myself today. Once more, I’m truly sorry. Is there anything you’d like to ask me?
model.why: Defined follow-up with a timeframe, repeated apology, and space for questions

model.text: No. Thank you for telling me straight. I’d rather know.

social.t: An error by the people she relies on can shake a long-term patient’s confidence in all her care. Honest disclosure, continuity and prompt follow-up help rebuild it.
Same-day bloods or a hospital visit need transport and support. Ask what she needs to get there rather than assuming.

legal.t: CQC Regulation 20 (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014): for a notifiable safety incident the practice must notify the person, give a true account, apologise, set out further enquiries, confirm it in writing and keep records.
An apology is not an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006, section 2). She may raise a complaint or claim; tell her how to do so and document the conversation accurately.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and the GMC and NMC guidance on the professional duty of candour (2015): be open, apologise, explain, and act to put matters right. Do not delay disclosure while an investigation happens.

Report through local systems and the Learn from Patient Safety Events service, hold a significant event analysis, search for other affected patients, and apply MHRA advice (September 2020) to state the weekly day in full on prescriptions.

community.t: Involve the dispensing pharmacy in the review, and use pharmacist counselling and the methotrexate patient card or booklet to reinforce weekly dosing.
Signpost the practice complaints process and independent patient-safety charities or advocacy if she wants support outside the practice.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, sore throat or feeling suddenly unwell — possible neutropenic sepsis
Mouth ulcers, vomiting or diarrhoea — mucositis and GI toxicity
Bruising, bleeding, new cough or breathlessness — marrow suppression or pneumonitis
psychosocial: How she can get to same-day bloods or hospital today
Her emotional response: shock, fear, anger, self-blame
Any interacting medicines on her list that raise toxicity risk
ice: Idea: “I took it like it said — have I done something wrong?”
Concern: “Is it serious? Am I going to be alright?” and anger at being let down
Expectation: an honest explanation, to know she is safe, and that it won’t happen again

playbook.diagnosis: A prescribing error has led to about six days of daily methotrexate, which risks serious toxicity even without symptoms: “This was our mistake. It can be serious, so we act today — stop the tablets, bloods this afternoon, and specialist advice.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Methotrexate is a strong medicine that the body needs a full week to clear. Taking it every day lets it build up, a bit like filling a bath faster than it can drain. We need to check how full the bath is today and, if needed, give a treatment that protects you.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you took it just as the label said — you did, and that’s exactly why this is our fault, not yours. And you’re right to be cross; you trusted us.”
management.psychosocial: Make the same-day plan workable for her (transport, who can help), give her one direct contact, and promise a timed call-back so she is not left waiting in fear.
sharedPlan: Stop methotrexate now; keep the box for checking
Same-day FBC, U&E, LFTs; urgent specialist advice on folinic acid rescue and admission
Incident report, significant event analysis, check other patients; written account and offer to meet
safetyNet: Fever, sore mouth or throat, bleeding, bruising, breathlessness or feeling unwell — 999 or A&E, mentioning methotrexate
Call-back within the hour and results chased the same day

pitfalls.intro: This station tests two things at once: honest disclosure and urgent clinical action. Candidates fail by doing one well and the other badly — a warm apology with no same-day bloods, or a sharp toxicity plan delivered defensively.

items.fail: Disclosing the error but then arranging bloods “later this week” because she feels well.
items.why: Methotrexate toxicity can develop before symptoms. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice” — delay in a potentially fatal overdose is unsafe.
items.fix: Stop the drug, same-day bloods, and specialist advice in the same call. Say why: “The blood effects can come before you feel anything.”

items.fail: A defensive or passive account — “the system produced the wrong label”, “the pharmacy should have noticed”.
items.why: Examiners read deflection as failure to take responsibility. The duty of candour needs a true account and a sincere apology from the practice.
items.fix: “That was our error, and I’m sorry.” Then explain what you are doing about it.

items.fail: Missing the self-blame cue: she says “I took it like it said” and the doctor moves straight to blood tests.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Unresolved self-blame colours the rest of the call.
items.fix: Pause and say explicitly: “You did nothing wrong. You followed the label exactly.”

items.fail: No toxicity screen — the doctor never asks about mouth ulcers, fever, bleeding or breathlessness.
items.why: Without it there is no basis for deciding urgency, and red flags already present would be missed.
items.fix: Ask the five: sore mouth or throat, vomiting or diarrhoea, fever, bruising or bleeding, breathlessness.

items.fail: Jargon such as “myelosuppression”, “mucositis” and “folinic acid rescue” without explanation.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.” A frightened patient on the phone cannot see your face to read reassurance.
items.fix: “It can lower your blood counts, which fight infection and stop bleeding. There’s a treatment that protects against that.”

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll be in touch” — no named red flags, no direct line, no timeframe.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and follow-up are standard failing feedback, and here they are clinically dangerous.
items.fix: Named red flags with a 999/A&E route, a direct number, and “I’ll ring you back within the hour”.

items.fail: Never mentioning what the practice will do to stop it happening again.
items.why: Candour includes the learning. Patients consistently ask whether it could happen to someone else.
items.fix: Name the incident report, the significant event analysis, the check on other patients, and a written follow-up.

timeMap.d: Confirm who you are speaking to. Say in the first minute that you are calling about a mistake with her medication.
Plain account: weekly drug, labelled daily, about six days taken. “That was our error and I’m sorry.” Lift the self-blame at once.
Mouth ulcers, sore throat, vomiting or diarrhoea, fever, bruising or bleeding, breathlessness. Stop the tablets and keep the box.
Same-day bloods, specialist advice, folinic acid or admission if advised. Respond to fear and anger. Explain the incident report and system fix.
999/A&E red flags, direct line, timed call-back, teach-back, offer to meet and a written account.

wordPics.fail: Vague or delayed disclosure (“there may have been a small issue”); no clear apology or a defensive one; accepts that she feels fine and plans routine bloods; no mention of stopping the drug or specialist advice; ignores her self-blame and anger; no red flags or follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Discloses the error clearly and apologises; stops methotrexate; arranges same-day bloods and specialist advice; screens for toxicity symptoms; tells her it was not her fault; gives red flags and a way to contact the practice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: confirms identity first; explains risk honestly but calmly; names folinic acid and possible admission as protection, not punishment; welcomes her anger without defending; explains the incident report, significant event analysis and the check on other patients; offers a meeting and written account; uses teach-back and a timed call-back.

avoid.dont: “There seems to have been a slight mix-up with the pharmacy label.”
avoid.instead: “Your prescription had the wrong instructions — daily instead of weekly. That was our error, and I’m very sorry.”
avoid.why: Minimising and shifting blame breaches the duty of candour and destroys trust.

avoid.dont: “You should have known it was a weekly tablet.”
avoid.instead: “You followed the label exactly. This is not your fault in any way.”
avoid.why: Blaming the patient is unprofessional and adds harm to harm.

avoid.dont: “As you feel fine, let’s check your bloods next week.”
avoid.instead: “The blood effects can come before any symptoms, so I want tests and specialist advice today.”
avoid.why: Delay on the grounds of feeling well is a clinical-management fail in a potentially fatal overdose.

That’s good to hear. The blood effects can show up before you feel anything, though, so we still need to act today. Do you still have the tablets with you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why feeling well does not remove the need to act

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, the box is here in the kitchen.
Please don’t take any more — stop them from now. Put the box to one side so it can be checked. Are you taking any other medicines at the moment that I should know about?
SCA_MODELS.why: Stops the drug, secures the supply and checks for interacting medicines

SCA_MODELS.text: Just what’s on my list at the surgery.

Here’s what I’d like to happen today. You need blood tests this afternoon to check your blood count, kidneys and liver. I’m also going to speak to the hospital specialist team straight after this call. There’s an antidote-type treatment called folinic acid that they may want to give, and they may prefer to see you at the hospital today to be safe. Can you get there if needed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day bloods and specialist advice; names folinic acid rescue and possible admission

SCA_MODELS.text: I can get there, yes. Hospital, though? That frightens me.

I understand — it sounds alarming. Going in doesn’t mean something bad has happened; it means we’re being careful because the mistake was ours and we want to catch any effect early. What’s going through your mind right now?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges fear and invites her feelings rather than rushing on

SCA_MODELS.text: I just trusted you. I’m shaken, and a bit cross, honestly.
You have every right to feel cross. You trusted us and we let you down. I’m not going to make excuses — I’m going to make sure you’re safe and keep you informed at every step.
SCA_MODELS.why: Accepts her anger without defensiveness and takes responsibility for the practice

SCA_MODELS.text: I also want you to know what happens next on our side. We’re reporting this as a patient-safety incident, we’ll look at exactly how the wrong instructions got through, and we’re checking no one else has been affected. I’ll write to you with what we find and what we change, and I’d like to offer you a meeting in person once you’re safe.
SCA_MODELS.why: Commits to reporting, significant event analysis, checking other patients and written follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d want to know it can’t happen to anyone else.
That’s exactly what we want too, and I’ll tell you what we’ve changed. In future your prescription will state the day of the week you take it, written in full.
SCA_MODELS.why: Links her request to a concrete safeguard

SCA_MODELS.text: Until you’re seen, if you get a temperature, shivers or feel suddenly unwell, a sore mouth or throat, bleeding or bruising, or breathlessness — ring 999 or go straight to A&E and tell them you’ve had extra methotrexate. I’ll give you my direct line for anything else.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific toxicity and sepsis red flags with a clear route

SCA_MODELS.text: All right. I’ll write that down.
Could you tell me back what you’re going to do this afternoon, just so I know I’ve explained it well?
No more tablets, blood test today, wait for your call about the hospital, and 999 if I get a temperature or bleeding.

That’s exactly right. I’ll ring you back within the hour once I’ve spoken to the specialists, and I’ll chase your results myself today. Once more, I’m truly sorry. Is there anything you’d like to ask me?
SCA_MODELS.why: Defined follow-up with a timeframe, repeated apology, and space for questions

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you for telling me straight. I’d rather know.

SCA_STEM.name: Maureen Selby
pmh: Long-term condition treated with oral methotrexate (intended once-weekly dosing)
meds: Methotrexate tablets — intended ONCE WEEKLY; most recent issue labelled as a DAILY dose
SCA_STEM.recent: Prescribing error identified: methotrexate issued with daily instead of weekly directions. Records suggest she has taken it daily for about 6 days. No recent bloods on this issue. No contact from her reporting symptoms.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: you are ringing her to disclose the error and act on the clinical risk today.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020) — methotrexate once-weekly · CQC Regulation 20 duty of candour · GMC and NMC professional duty of candour (2015) · NICE NG253 (sepsis)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Daily instead of weekly methotrexate is a recognised, potentially fatal error. Stop it, get same-day bloods and specialist advice, and disclose it openly with an apology in the same call.

points.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020): methotrexate for autoimmune disease is taken once a week, and fatal overdoses continue to be reported from daily dosing. Toxicity includes mucositis, diarrhoea and vomiting, bone-marrow suppression (neutropenic sepsis, bleeding), liver injury, renal impairment and pneumonitis. Symptoms may lag behind blood changes, so feeling well is not reassurance.

Stop methotrexate now and remove the remaining supply. Arrange same-day FBC, U&E and LFTs with clinical assessment, and seek urgent specialist advice (acute medical or rheumatology team, using TOXBASE/National Poisons Information Service guidance). Calcium folinate rescue and admission are specialist decisions — doses per BNF and specialist advice.

Neutropenia after methotrexate overdose can present as fever or simply feeling unwell. Any fever, rigors, sore throat or feeling acutely unwell needs emergency assessment as possible neutropenic sepsis (NICE NG253 for people aged 16 and over).

CQC Regulation 20 applies to registered providers, including GP practices. For a notifiable safety incident (one that has caused, or might cause, moderate or severe harm or death) the practice must tell the person, give a true account, apologise, explain what enquiries will follow, confirm it in writing and keep a record. CQC expects the notification in person; an urgent phone call is right here, followed by an offer to meet and a written account.

GMC and NMC guidance on the professional duty of candour (2015) and GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): be open and honest, apologise, explain the short- and long-term effects, and put matters right. An apology is not an admission of legal liability (Compensation Act 2006, section 2; NHS Resolution “Saying sorry”, 2017).

Record and report the incident (local reporting and the national Learn from Patient Safety Events service), hold a significant event analysis, check that no other patient has received the same directions, and fix the safeguard. MHRA advice: agree the day of the week with the patient and write it in full on the prescription.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity, checked it was a good time to talk, and stated the purpose of the call plainly at the outset.
Ability to attend today, practical support, and how she is coping with the shock.
Picked up “I took it like it said” (self-blame) and “I’m a bit cross” (anger), and responded to each.
Her understanding of the error, her fear of harm, her anger at being let down, and what she wants to happen.
Same-day FBC, U&E and LFTs with clinical assessment; tablets retained for checking.
Screens for mucositis, GI toxicity, marrow suppression, liver or renal injury and pneumonitis; asks about interacting medicines.
Recognises possible neutropenic sepsis and bleeding risk; does not accept “I feel fine” as reassurance.
States clearly: a prescribing error with around six days of daily methotrexate, potentially serious, currently without symptoms.
Stop the drug now, same-day bloods, urgent specialist advice (folinic acid rescue, possible admission), with her agreement.
Fulfils the duty of candour: apology, true account, incident report, significant event analysis, checks other patients, written follow-up.
Named red flags with 999/A&E route, direct contact number, timed call-back, and results chased the same day.

social.t: An error by the people she relies on can shake a long-term patient’s confidence in all her care. Honest disclosure, continuity and prompt follow-up help rebuild it.
Same-day bloods or a hospital visit need transport and support. Ask what she needs to get there rather than assuming.

legal.t: CQC Regulation 20 (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014): for a notifiable safety incident the practice must notify the person, give a true account, apologise, set out further enquiries, confirm it in writing and keep records.
An apology is not an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006, section 2). She may raise a complaint or claim; tell her how to do so and document the conversation accurately.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and the GMC and NMC guidance on the professional duty of candour (2015): be open, apologise, explain, and act to put matters right. Do not delay disclosure while an investigation happens.

Report through local systems and the Learn from Patient Safety Events service, hold a significant event analysis, search for other affected patients, and apply MHRA advice (September 2020) to state the weekly day in full on prescriptions.

community.t: Involve the dispensing pharmacy in the review, and use pharmacist counselling and the methotrexate patient card or booklet to reinforce weekly dosing.
Signpost the practice complaints process and independent patient-safety charities or advocacy if she wants support outside the practice.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, sore throat or feeling suddenly unwell — possible neutropenic sepsis
Mouth ulcers, vomiting or diarrhoea — mucositis and GI toxicity
Bruising, bleeding, new cough or breathlessness — marrow suppression or pneumonitis
psychosocial: How she can get to same-day bloods or hospital today
Her emotional response: shock, fear, anger, self-blame
Any interacting medicines on her list that raise toxicity risk
ice: Idea: “I took it like it said — have I done something wrong?”
Concern: “Is it serious? Am I going to be alright?” and anger at being let down
Expectation: an honest explanation, to know she is safe, and that it won’t happen again

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: A prescribing error has led to about six days of daily methotrexate, which risks serious toxicity even without symptoms: “This was our mistake. It can be serious, so we act today — stop the tablets, bloods this afternoon, and specialist advice.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Methotrexate is a strong medicine that the body needs a full week to clear. Taking it every day lets it build up, a bit like filling a bath faster than it can drain. We need to check how full the bath is today and, if needed, give a treatment that protects you.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you took it just as the label said — you did, and that’s exactly why this is our fault, not yours. And you’re right to be cross; you trusted us.”
management.psychosocial: Make the same-day plan workable for her (transport, who can help), give her one direct contact, and promise a timed call-back so she is not left waiting in fear.
sharedPlan: Stop methotrexate now; keep the box for checking
Same-day FBC, U&E, LFTs; urgent specialist advice on folinic acid rescue and admission
Incident report, significant event analysis, check other patients; written account and offer to meet
safetyNet: Fever, sore mouth or throat, bleeding, bruising, breathlessness or feeling unwell — 999 or A&E, mentioning methotrexate
Call-back within the hour and results chased the same day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests two things at once: honest disclosure and urgent clinical action. Candidates fail by doing one well and the other badly — a warm apology with no same-day bloods, or a sharp toxicity plan delivered defensively.

items.fail: Disclosing the error but then arranging bloods “later this week” because she feels well.
items.why: Methotrexate toxicity can develop before symptoms. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice” — delay in a potentially fatal overdose is unsafe.
items.fix: Stop the drug, same-day bloods, and specialist advice in the same call. Say why: “The blood effects can come before you feel anything.”

items.fail: A defensive or passive account — “the system produced the wrong label”, “the pharmacy should have noticed”.
items.why: Examiners read deflection as failure to take responsibility. The duty of candour needs a true account and a sincere apology from the practice.
items.fix: “That was our error, and I’m sorry.” Then explain what you are doing about it.

items.fail: Missing the self-blame cue: she says “I took it like it said” and the doctor moves straight to blood tests.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Unresolved self-blame colours the rest of the call.
items.fix: Pause and say explicitly: “You did nothing wrong. You followed the label exactly.”

items.fail: No toxicity screen — the doctor never asks about mouth ulcers, fever, bleeding or breathlessness.
items.why: Without it there is no basis for deciding urgency, and red flags already present would be missed.
items.fix: Ask the five: sore mouth or throat, vomiting or diarrhoea, fever, bruising or bleeding, breathlessness.

items.fail: Jargon such as “myelosuppression”, “mucositis” and “folinic acid rescue” without explanation.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.” A frightened patient on the phone cannot see your face to read reassurance.
items.fix: “It can lower your blood counts, which fight infection and stop bleeding. There’s a treatment that protects against that.”

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll be in touch” — no named red flags, no direct line, no timeframe.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and follow-up are standard failing feedback, and here they are clinically dangerous.
items.fix: Named red flags with a 999/A&E route, a direct number, and “I’ll ring you back within the hour”.

items.fail: Never mentioning what the practice will do to stop it happening again.
items.why: Candour includes the learning. Patients consistently ask whether it could happen to someone else.
items.fix: Name the incident report, the significant event analysis, the check on other patients, and a written follow-up.
